messages.subject: more logistic regression
parts:
Hi,

I'd like to follow up on the logistic regression thread with the
following question: What does it mean if the intercept is significant?
Is it just that the numbers of successes and failures are uneven, or
is there something more to it? Does it matter? Would it be ok to
generate a random sample of the larger group to have equal amounts of
successes and failures, and would that take care of the problem, if
there is one?

Thanks, --Martin

messages.author: 3edc58ee737edd94
messages.subject: Re: more logistic regression
parts:
Unfortunately, I don't have a quick answer to that myself (and I am
traveling right now so can't try and look it up). Off the top of my
head, I can say this: in linear regression, if an intercept is
significant, it differs significantly from zero, which for many corpus-
linguistic applications at least is probably not too relevant an
issue. I would assume that for logistic regression the meaning of a
significant intercept is something similar and thus unproblematic,
probably not too important, and certainly not requiring any tweaking
of the sample sizes.
HTH,
STG
